sections.h: Gods made of stone and bronze
sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus mocks idols in the prophets' manner: one is a stone 'like the stone people walk on', another bronze 'no better than the vessels hammered out for our use', another rotting wood or rusting iron (2:2). A craftsman could have made the same material into pots (2:3, with Lake's note). The gold and silver gods are locked up at night and guarded by day, the cheap ones left out (2:7). 'You bow down to these, and you end up becoming just like them' (2:5), as Psalm 115:8 warns.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 2:1-10; Psalm 115:4-8; Isaiah 44:9-20; Jeremiah 10:3-5

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus calls the Jewish food laws 'jumpy fear about foods' and asks how it can be anything but 'lawless' to accept some of God's creatures and refuse others (4:1-2). Its conclusion, that Christians need not keep them, has New Testament roots (Mark 7:19; 1 Timothy 4:4); its scorn for those who keep them does not. See the note at 4:1.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 4:1-2; Mark 7:19; 1 Timothy 4:3-4; Leviticus 11:1-47

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus lists 'their superstition about the Sabbath' among Jewish practices 'not worth a word' and accuses Jews of slandering God 'as if he forbade doing any good thing on the Sabbath day' (4:1, 3), turning the Gospels' debates about healing on the Sabbath (Mark 3:4; Matthew 12:12) into a charge against all Jews. It says nothing about which day Christians kept.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 4:1; Epistle to Diognetus 4:3; Mark 3:4; Matthew 12:12

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus mocks circumcision as 'the cutting short of the flesh' and denies that it is 'proof that they are chosen' (4:1, 4). Paul had attacked those who required it of Gentiles (Philippians 3:2) and taught circumcision of the heart (Romans 2:29), but he calls it the seal of Abraham's faith (Romans 4:11), where Genesis calls it 'the sign of the covenant' (Genesis 17:11).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 4:4; Philippians 3:2; Romans 2:28-29; Romans 4:11; Genesis 17:11

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus says that God, 'who made heaven and earth and all that is in them', needs none of the things he gives (3:4), and that those who honor him with blood, fat and whole burnt offerings are no different from those who make offerings to deaf idols (3:5; compare the 'blood and the smoke of burning fat' of the Greek altars, 2:8). It goes further than Psalm 50, Isaiah 1 or Hebrews 10, which criticize or fulfill the offerings but do not call them idolatry; see the canon note at 3:5.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 2:8; Epistle to Diognetus 3:3-5; Psalm 50:9-13; Hebrews 10:1-4; Acts 17:25

sections.b: Writing to a pagan, the author of the Epistle to Diognetus calls Jewish religion 'superstition' (1:1), treats the temple sacrifices as no better than offerings to idols (3:5), and dismisses the food laws, Sabbath, circumcision and feasts as 'laughable and not worth a word' (4:1), the 'fussing and the boasting of the Jews' (4:6). He grants that the Jews worship the one God (3:2). He says Jews 'make war' on Christians 'as foreigners' (5:17). He never says that God gave Israel these laws. The note at 4:1 weighs the passage against the Bible (Romans 9:4; Romans 11:28-29) and gives the Catholic Church's teaching in Nostra Aetate 4 that 'the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God'.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 1:1; Epistle to Diognetus 3:2-5; Epistle to Diognetus 4:1-6; Epistle to Diognetus 5:17; Romans 9:4; Romans 11:28-29

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus grants that the Jews rightly 'honor one God of all things' (3:2) but says their worship is wrong in form (3-4); it never speaks of Israel's covenant or future. The separate homily at its end says of the Word that 'the people dishonored him; apostles preached him; the nations believed in him' (11:3), where Lake notes that 'the people' is 'the chosen people of Israel, in contrast with ... the heathen nations'.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 3:2; Epistle to Diognetus 11:3; John 1:11; Romans 11:11

sections.h: 'They do not throw away their newborn children'
sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus says Christians 'marry; they have children; but their newborn children they do not throw away' (5:6), a mark that set them apart in a world where unwanted infants were exposed. Justin Martyr told the emperor the same: 'to expose newly-born children is the part of wicked men' (First Apology 27).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 5:6; Didache 2:2

sections.h: A shared table, not a shared bed
sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus describes Christians as marrying 'like all others' and having children (5:6), and as open-handed but faithful: 'They set out a shared table, but not a shared bed' (5:7). 'Bed' (koitēn) is Maranus's conjecture, which Lake prints and renders 'They offer free hospitality, but guard their purity'; the manuscript repeats 'common' (koinēn), which Otto (1879) took to mean a shared table, but not an unclean one (see the variant at 5:7).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 5:6-7; Hebrews 13:2-4

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus applies the language of the resident foreigner to Christians everywhere: 'They live in their own homelands, but as resident aliens' (5:5). That theme, from Abraham to 1 Peter and the early church, has its own page, Strangers and Exiles (resident-aliens); this page keeps Israel's law and practice toward foreigners.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 5:5; 1 Peter 2:11; Genesis 23:4

sections.h: Obeying the laws and going beyond them
sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus pictures Christians as model citizens: 'They obey the laws that have been laid down, and by the way they live they outdo the laws' (5:10), while their real citizenship is in heaven (5:9). God has 'stationed them at a post' they may not refuse (6:10), and God himself does not compel: 'force has no place in God' (7:4). The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes 5:5, 5:10 and 6:10 on the duties of citizens (2240).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 5:5-10; Epistle to Diognetus 6:10; Epistle to Diognetus 7:4; Romans 13:1-7; 1 Peter 2:13-17

sections.b: Paul's 'we belong to a commonwealth in heaven' (Philippians 3:20) is taken up in the Epistle to Diognetus: Christians 'pass their days on earth, but they live as citizens of heaven' (5:9), with the same root word (politeuontai); Lake's margin points to Philippians 3:18-20.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 5:9; Philippians 3:20; Philippians 1:27

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus builds its sixth chapter on one likeness: 'what the soul is to a body, that is what Christians are in the world' (6:1). The soul is invisible, hated by the flesh, shut up in the body yet holding it together, 'immortal ... in a mortal tent' (6:4-8). The picture of the body as the soul's prison sits uneasily with Genesis and with Paul's hope of the body's resurrection; see the canon note at 6:5.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 6:1-9; 1 Peter 2:11; 2 Corinthians 5:1-4; 1 Corinthians 15:42-44

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus never names Jesus but speaks of 'the holy Word', whom God sent: not an angel or ruler but 'the very Craftsman and Creator of the universe', by whom he made the heavens and whom the sun, moon and stars obey (7:2), sent 'as God' and 'as a human being to human beings' (7:4). The separate homily at its end (11-12) speaks of the Word who 'appeared', 'was from the beginning', 'was discovered to be old, and is always being born young in the hearts of the saints' (11:2-4), echoing John 1 and 1 John 1:1.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 7:2-4; Epistle to Diognetus 11:2-5; John 1:1-14; 1 John 1:1

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus mocks 'trustworthy' philosophers who said God is fire, or water, or another element God made (8:2): a target that includes the Stoic teaching of God as a fiery reason running through the world. Its aside, 'they call God the very thing they are about to go into', may glance at the Stoic end of the world in fire (see the note there).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 8:2-4; Acts 17:18; Wisdom of Solomon 13:1-2

sections.h: 'No one knew God until he came'
sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus says that before Christ came no one knew 'at all what God is' (8:1) and that 'no human being has seen him or known him. But he has shown himself' through faith (8:5-6). It allows less than Paul (Romans 1:19-20) and much less than Justin Martyr, who said that 'those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists' (First Apology 46). See the canon note at 8:1.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 8:1-6; Romans 1:19-20; Acts 14:17

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus has its own passage on the cross: God 'handed over his own Son, a ransom on our behalf: the holy for the lawless, the blameless for the wicked, the righteous for the unrighteous' (9:2); 'what else had the power to cover our sins, except his righteousness?' (9:3); 'Oh, the sweet exchange! ... That the lawlessness of many should be hidden in one righteous man, and the righteousness of one should justify many who are lawless!' (9:5). It echoes Mark 10:45, 1 Peter 3:18 and 2 Corinthians 5:21 and gives no further theory of how the exchange works.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 9:1-6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 3:18; Mark 10:45; 1 Timothy 2:6

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus asks, 'In whom could we, lawless and ungodly as we were, be justified, except in the Son of God alone?' (9:4), and says the righteousness of one 'should justify many who are lawless' (9:5), after God had let humanity prove 'by our own deeds' that it was 'unworthy of life' (9:1). The language is Paul's (Romans 5:18-19) and Isaiah's (Isaiah 53:11).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 9:1-5; Romans 3:21-26; Romans 5:18-19; Isaiah 53:11

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus points Diognetus to the martyrs: thrown to wild beasts to make them deny the Lord, they are not overcome, and 'the more of them are punished', the more others join (7:7-8); 'This is God's power' (7:9). Those who come to know 'that other fire' will admire those who endure 'the fire that lasts a short time' (10:7-8), the contrast Polycarp drew before his own burning (Martyrdom of Polycarp 11:2).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 6:9; Epistle to Diognetus 7:7-9; Epistle to Diognetus 10:7-8; Martyrdom of Polycarp 11:2

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus says God sent his Son first in love, 'not in judgment', but 'he will send him to judge, and who will remain standing at his coming?' (7:5-6; Malachi 3:2). The real death is 'kept for those who will be condemned to the eternal fire, which will punish to the end those handed over to it' (10:7); the note there discusses 'to the end'.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 7:5-6; Epistle to Diognetus 10:7; Malachi 3:2; Matthew 25:41

sections.b: The homily at the end of the Epistle to Diognetus reads Eden's two trees as meant to go together: 'there is no life without knowledge, and no safe knowledge without true life. That is why the two were planted side by side' (12:4). 'The tree of knowledge does not kill; disobedience kills' (12:2). Those who love God rightly become 'a paradise of delight' with a fruitful tree growing in them (12:1).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 12:1-8; Genesis 2:9; Genesis 3:22-24; Revelation 2:7

sections.b: The homily of Epistle to Diognetus 11-12 uses the Greek Genesis's name for Eden, 'paradise of delight' (Genesis 3:23-24 in the Septuagint), for believers themselves: those who love God rightly 'become a paradise of delight' (12:1), where the snake cannot reach (12:8).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 12:1-3; Epistle to Diognetus 12:8; Genesis 3:23-24

sections.h: A mystery not learned from humans
sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus says the 'mystery' of the Christians' reverence for God cannot be learned from a human being (4:6); God kept his plan 'in a mystery' and seemed not to care, then revealed it through his beloved Child (8:10-11). Christians are not entrusted with 'a plan of merely human mysteries' (7:1), and those who believe 'will begin to speak of God's mysteries' (10:7).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 4:6; Epistle to Diognetus 7:1; Epistle to Diognetus 8:10-11; Epistle to Diognetus 10:7; Romans 16:25

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus lists God's gifts to humans: reason, mind, the right to look up to him, and that 'he formed them from his own image' (10:2), using the Greek verb of Genesis 2:7 for the forming of Adam. The image is the ground for imitating God (10:4-6).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 10:2-6; Genesis 1:26-27; Genesis 2:7

sections.h: 'A god to those who receive it'
sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus says that whoever takes up a neighbor's burden and 'passes on to the needy what he has received from God' becomes 'a god to those who receive it' and is 'an imitator of God' (10:6); not wealth or power over others (10:5).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 10:4-6; Galatians 6:2; Acts 20:35

sections.b: The homily at the end of the Epistle to Diognetus says that where the tree of life is kept, 'Eve is not corrupted, but a virgin is trusted' (12:8): either Mary, who believed (Luke 1:45), set against Eve, as Justin Martyr had done (Dialogue with Trypho 100), or the believer kept as a pure virgin for Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2-3).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 12:8; Luke 1:38; Luke 1:45; 2 Corinthians 11:2-3

sections.b: The homily at the end of the Epistle to Diognetus names 'the Lord's Passover' (12:9), the Christian Pascha; Lake reports Otto's view that it was an Easter homily.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 12:9; 1 Corinthians 5:7

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus mocks Jews who 'keep close watch on the stars and the moon to observe the months and the days' and 'carve up God's plans and the changes of the seasons' into feasts and times of mourning (4:5), while praising the moon that obeys the Word (7:2).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 4:5; Epistle to Diognetus 7:2; Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16

sections.h: Sent as God, as a human being to human beings
sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus, never naming Jesus, says God sent his Word, the Creator of all, 'in forbearance and gentleness. As a king sends his son, he sent him as a king. He sent him as God. He sent him as a human being to human beings' (7:4). It does not explain how; it says why: 'to save and to persuade, not to force. For force has no place in God.' The homily joined to it adds that the Word 'appeared as new, was discovered to be old, and is always being born young in the hearts of the saints' (11:4).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 7:2-5; Epistle to Diognetus 11:3-5; John 1:14

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus calls the one God sent his 'servant' (Greek pais, which can also mean 'child'; 8:9, 11; 9:1) and his 'own Son' (9:2), 'his only Son' (10:2), sent 'as God' and 'as a human being' (7:4). The homily of chapters 11-12 calls the Word 'the one who always is, who today is reckoned as Son' (11:5), with Psalm 2:7.
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 7:4; Epistle to Diognetus 8:9-11; Epistle to Diognetus 9:1-2; Epistle to Diognetus 11:5; Psalm 2:7
